metadata.file_name: The  Non Impact of Differential Test Taker Engagement on Aggregated Scores.pdf
metadata.title: (The (Non)Impact of Differential Test Taker Engagement on Aggregated Scores)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses pilot administration data from the PISA-Based Test for Schools (PBTS) in the United States, with 15-year-old students sampled from 84 schools. The methodology describes item-response-time classification (RTE/RBE) and subsequent aggregation to school-level performance and distortion scores, followed by descriptive statistics and a random-intercept multilevel robustness check. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not name any weight variable. Because the analysis is based on a pilot dataset and the models are multilevel with school clustering, the results should be interpreted as descriptive/robustness evidence rather than population-representative estimates for all U.S. schools.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are PBTS scale scores and derived distortion scores computed from standard versus effort-moderated scoring, along with engagement indices (RBE) aggregated to the school level. These are not analyzed as PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes in the PISA sense (i.e., the paper does not describe plausible values draws or PV pooling). Missing-data handling is not described because the analysis pipeline is primarily based on response-time classification and score computation; the manuscript does not document any explicit missingness rule for students/items/schools, which is a reporting gap for transparency.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The dataset is the one used by Wise and Gao (2017) from the pilot administration of the computer-based PBTS. The pilot included 5,091 15-year-old students from 84 schools in the United States. The current study classifies each item response as solution behavior versus non-effortful behavior using response-time thresholds (10% normative threshold method) and computes student-level RBE, standard PBTS scores, effort-moderated scores, and distortion (standard minus effort-moderated). The analysis then aggregates student-level measures within each school to produce school-level engagement and performance indicators; the paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the pilot dataset construction.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA the study leveraged Response time effort (RBE), Score distortion (standard-effort), Effort-moderated PBTS score to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study analyzes pilot computer-based PISA-Based Test for Schools (PBTS) data administered to 5,091 U.S. students (15-year-olds) across 84 schools, using response-time-based engagement measures. Engagement is operationalized via response behavior effort (RBE), defined as the proportion of item responses classified as solution behaviors using response-time thresholds; the study also computes effort-moderated PBTS scores and a distortion score (standard minus effort-moderated) to quantify rapid-guessing-related score distortion. Results show that school-level mean engagement and mean performance are strongly positively correlated (r = 0.56–0.72 by subject), yet effort-moderated scoring produces almost no net shift in school means: standard versus effort-moderated school performance correlations are near-perfect (r > 0.999). A random-intercept multilevel robustness check indicates very small between-school variance in distortion (ICC up to 0.007 in reading), implying that differential disengagement has marginal impact on aggregated scores. The paper does not use machine learning models and does not report PV handling or a missing-data strategy, so findings are best interpreted as evidence about score robustness under low-stakes disengagement rather than predictive performance. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ML because the manuscript does not train or evaluate any machine learning predictive models; instead, it uses descriptive statistics and a random-intercept multilevel model as a robustness check. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms to populate and no ML target-variable performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) to extract. The study’s core contribution is methodological/empirical evidence about the stability of aggregated PBTS scores after removing rapid-guessing effects via effort-moderated scoring.
